edges.note: Aramaic-speaking Christianity reached Edessa early, but by what route and hands scholars genuinely disagree.
Egyptian Christianity's origins are obscure in detail, but its second-century emergence out of the same scattered network is broadly accepted.
The desert movement grew in Alexandria’s shadow; Athanasius of Alexandria wrote the Life of Antony that carried it to the world.
Jerome and Paula toured the Egyptian ascetic settlements; the circle's practice consciously imported the desert's renunciation.
Origen's textual scholarship (the Hexapla) is the direct ancestor of Jerome's Hebrew-testing project — even as Jerome turned publicly against Origen's theology.
Jerome heard Gregory of Nazianzus teach in Constantinople and calls him his teacher.
The School of Nisibis and the Persian church carry this world's teaching directly onward after 410.
Basil visited Egypt; the whole Greek monastic tradition claims the desert as its root.
John Cassian carried the desert's teaching to Gaul; Benedict's Rule commends his Conferences by name.
Via Gaul (Lérins, Martin of Tours); the route is secure in outline, thinner in specifics.
Post-Chalcedon Egyptian Christianity is the direct continuation of the desert tradition.
The Waldensians adhered to the Reformation in 1532; how much earlier “proto-Protestant” continuity is real versus retrospective is a live scholarly argument.
The Radical Reformation defined itself against the magisterial reformers' church-state settlement as much as against Rome.
Azusa Street's leaders and vocabulary came directly out of the Holiness movement.
Aladura and Zionist movements drew on Pentecostal currents while being genuinely African-initiated — the balance is actively studied.
The Holiness movement understood itself as recovering Wesley's own doctrine of sanctification.

movements.name: Donatism
movements.statusDescription: One of the worlds chosen for its era after a completed survey. Construction has not begun.
movements.sourcing: Substantial but heavily via opponents (Augustine) - a named challenge
movements.relationsSummary: Rival-sibling of the Latin pastoral world; martyr-memory identity
movements.why: This world has already been chosen — and it may surprise you that it's here: the churches of Roman North Africa that broke communion with their neighbors over what faithfulness under persecution required, kept their own bishops for a century, and built their identity on the memory of the martyrs. History mostly remembers them through their opponents — Augustine wrote against them, and the label "Donatist" was never their own name for themselves. That is exactly why this project chose them: a whole communion of real Christians, serious about holiness, known mainly through hostile pens, deserves to speak as itself. Construction has not yet begun.

Nothing about it was judged too hard or too thin — it was selected on the strength of its sources; construction simply has not begun.

movements.why: This world has already been chosen: the church that woke up one morning allied to the empire that had been killing it — Constantine's alliance, Ambrose facing down an emperor at the church door, popes building the machinery of a church that could outlast Rome itself. It is the era's least comfortable world and one of its most consequential: power, and what power does to a community formed by a crucified Lord, held honestly as the sources hold it. Construction has not yet begun.
